findings.scenario: Run the probe with no flags. cli.js passes { baseUrl: undefined, retries: undefined, timeoutMs: undefined }. findings.title: Missing-account branch throws without releasing the lock
findings.quote: throw new PayoutError(`payout ${payoutId} has no bank account`);
findings.scenario: sendPayout is called for a payout with no accountNumber. The lock for payout:<id> is acquired on line 5, then the branch on lines 7-10 marks the payout failed and throws. release() is never called, because it only runs in the finally block that starts on line 11. In src/locks.js, held.delete(key) runs only inside release(), so the key stays in the held map. The next acquire for the same payoutId loops on held.get(key).promise, which never resolves, so the retry hangs forever.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The throw sits before the try/finally, so the finally cannot release the lock. No test in the diff covers this path, and locks.js has no timeout or expiry.

findings.title: payouts.get moved outside try, so a throw leaks the lock
findings.scenario: payouts.get rejects, for example on a database timeout, after acquire has succeeded. The error propagates out of sendPayout before the try block is entered, so release() never runs. Every later sendPayout for that payoutId then hangs in acquire.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The get call was inside try before this diff, so the finally covered it. The diff moved it out without moving the lock release along with it.

findings.title: Account check now runs before the 'sent' idempotency check
findings.scenario: A payout that was already sent has no accountNumber, for example because the account was cleared after sending. A retry now reaches this check before the status === 'sent' return on line 12, so the payout is overwritten to status 'failed' even though the transfer went out.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The diff does not show whether sent payouts keep accountNumber, and no test covers a sent payout without one.

findings.quote: throw new PayoutError(`payout ${payoutId} has no bank account`);

findings.title: Refund transfers money in the wrong direction
findings.scenario: A refund of 500 on an order from customer 'c1' calls transfer('store', 'c1', 500). In ledger.js, transfer(toAccountId, fromAccountId, amountCents) debits the second argument and credits the first, so 'c1' loses 500 and 'store' gains 500. The customer is charged instead of refunded. payouts.js uses the correct order, transfer(seller.accountId, STORE_ACCOUNT, amountCents).
findings.whyNotPrevented: transfer takes two untyped string account IDs with no names at the call site, and no test covers refundOrder or checks balances after a refund. The positive-amount check in ledger.js does not catch swapped accounts.

findings.title: Saved preferences leak into the shared defaults object and into other users' responses
findings.scenario: User A has savedPreferences {"theme":"dark"}. preferencesFor(A) runs and sets DEFAULT_PREFERENCES.theme to 'dark', because defaultPreferences() in src/defaults.js:8 returns the module-level object itself, not a copy. Then user B with savedPreferences null calls preferencesFor(B) and gets theme 'dark' instead of 'light'. Every later response carries the previous user's values until the process restarts.

findings.scenario: A saved key such as "constructor" or "__proto__" passes the `in` check because it is inherited from Object.prototype. JSON.parse can produce an own "__proto__" key, so the assignment on line 13 can change the prototype of the object instead of ignoring the unsupported key.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The filter only checks membership with `in`. Nothing restricts it to the supported own keys.

findings.scenario: defaultPreferences() returns the module-level DEFAULT_PREFERENCES object itself (src/defaults.js line 8: return DEFAULT_PREFERENCES;). User A saves theme 'dark', and preferencesFor(A) assigns preferences.theme = 'dark' on that shared object. findings.whyNotPrevented: defaults.js returns the same object on each call instead of a copy, and preferences.js mutates the returned object. No test or type covers two calls in sequence, and nothing copies the object.
